money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: Croatia's currency is the euro (EUR). If you're travelling to or from any non-EU country, declare cash of more than 10,000 euros or equivalent. This covers all forms of currency, not only cash. If you fail to declare it or give wrong information, you'll be fined and the funds may be confiscated. You don't need to declare currency if you're travelling to or from another EU country.

laws.rule: Possessing, using or trafficking illicit drugs is illegal. If you're arrested for a drug offence, police may detain you while they investigate. Penalties include imprisonment.
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: Police issue on-the-spot fines for some minor offences, including traffic violations. They may detain you and/or hold your passport if you: challenge the offence can't pay the fine
laws.heading: On-the-spot fines

laws.rule: Foreigners buying property have been involved in lengthy disputes about the validity of property titles. Seek independent legal advice before signing any contracts.
laws.heading: Property laws

laws.rule: You must carry an ID, such as your passport, at all times. You must register your stay with the local police within 48 hours of arrival. If you're staying at a hotel or a tourist facility, the accommodation provider will register you. Drinking alcohol in public areas, outside bars and restaurants, and in popular tourist areas such as Split and Dubrovnik is prohibited. Signs warning of prohibited behaviours, including drunken and disorderly behaviour, have been put up, and on-the-spot fines are issued. Dress codes apply. Police may fine you if you're shirtless or wearing swimwear in towns with signs banning this.
laws.heading: Other laws

laws.rule: Court staff take holidays over the summer. If you're detained at that time, you may face delays in having your case processed. You may not be able to leave Croatia until the matter is finalised.
laws.heading: Court holidays

laws.rule: To drive a vehicle, you'll need both: a current Australian driver's licence, and a valid international driving permit (IDP) Driving without an IDP could void your travel and vehicle insurance. If you plan to live in Croatia, you must exchange your Australian driver's licence for a Croatian one within 12 months of arrival. You can do this at the local police station.
laws.heading: Driving permit

culture-and-protocol.dress_and_conduct: Carry your passport. Some town centres, including Split and Dubrovnik, give on-the-spot fines for drinking in public, sleeping in public, walking around shirtless or in swimwear, and climbing on monuments; public order offences such as shouting, drunkenness or insulting officials can bring fines up to 4,000 euros. Beware of unexploded mines in former war areas away from tourist resorts.
culture-and-protocol.note: From UK Government (FCDO) travel advice, written for British travellers but the laws apply to all visitors. Confirm locally.

visa-preparation.fastest_entry: Visa-free short stays (90 days or less) as part of the Schengen area, in some cases.
visa-preparation.before_departure: Nothing to lodge before travel today: EES registration happens at the border. ETIAS hadn't started on 2026-11-01.
steps: Croatia is in the Schengen area: short stays of 90 days or less can be visa-free in some cases; other purposes or longer stays need a visa before travel.
At the first Schengen border, give fingerprints and a photo for the Entry/Exit System (EES). It's free; nothing is needed before arrival, and sites charging for it are fraudulent.
Carry your passport when crossing borders, including inside Schengen (temporary internal checks are in place in places).
Get a clear entry stamp at the first Schengen entry.
